Fab
FAB
adjective (Boomer slang)
Clipped from fabulous (Latin fabulosus, celebrated in fable). Fab is British slang of the early 1960s, made world-famous by the Beatles, whom the Liverpool press and their press officer Tony Barrow dubbed "the Fab Four" in 1963; with Beatlemania it crossed to America in February 1964. It meant terrific, marvelous, and carried the whole bright, mop-topped optimism of 1964–65. It enjoyed a second life in the 1990s and 2000s (Queer Eye’s "Fab Five," 2003).

Biblical Definition

Fab is short for fabulous — marvelous, terrific, wonderful — and to Boomers it will forever mean the Beatles, the Fab Four, and the moment in February 1964 when seventy-three million Americans watched them on The Ed Sullivan Show. The Christian observation: the word’s root is worth a moment. Fabulous first meant "belonging to fable" — legendary, not real. Beatlemania was fabulous in both senses: marvelous, and built on a kind of legend, as screaming crowds made four young musicians into something like gods. John Lennon said as much in 1966, telling a London reporter that the Beatles were "more popular than Jesus now," and records were burned across the American South when the remark was reprinted. Whatever Lennon meant, the observation exposed something true about celebrity. Scripture records what happens when a crowd treats a man as divine: when Herod spoke, "the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory" (Act 12:22–23). "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm" (Jer 17:5). John’s closing words are the right word to every fan: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1Jn 5:21). The music can be enjoyed; the musicians can be admired; but the truly fabulous — the marvelous that is no fable — is the gospel, which Peter insisted was not "cunningly devised fables" but eyewitness truth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Early-1960s British slang (clipped fabulous) made famous by the Beatles, "the Fab Four" (1963) — a reminder that celebrity can become idolatry (Act 12:22–23; 1Jn 5:21), and that the true marvel is the gospel, which is no fable.

FAB, adj. (British slang, early 1960s; Boomer era) Fabulous; terrific; wonderful. "The Fab Four" — the Beatles (1963).

Webster (1828) — FABULOUS, adjective 1. Feigned, as a story; devised; fictitious; as a fabulous story; a fabulous description. 2. Related in fable; described or celebrated in fables; invented; not real; as a fabulous hero; the fabulous exploits of Hercules. 3. The fabulous age of Greece and Rome, was the early age of those countries, the accounts of which are mostly fabulous or in which the fabulous achievements of their heroes were performed; called also the heroic age.

Decode for families: fabulous once meant "fabled, unreal." Peter used the contrast: "we have not followed cunningly devised fables" (2Pe 1:16).

Key Scripture

Act 12:22 — "And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man."

Act 12:23 — "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost."

Jer 17:5 — "Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD."

1Jn 5:21 — "Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen."

Exo 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

Modern Corruption

Fab carried the joy of Beatlemania and also its idolatry of celebrity; Scripture warns against giving men the glory due to God and calls the gospel the one marvel that is no fable.

expand to see more

Beatlemania was something new: a mass devotion, mostly of teenage girls, expressed in screaming, fainting, and a kind of worship. The word fab was its liturgy. Older generations had their idols too — Sinatra had bobby-soxers — but television made the scale unprecedented, and the pattern has repeated with every pop phenomenon since. Lennon’s 1966 remark was arrogant, but it was also, sadly, a fair report on where the devotion of many young people had gone.

The Christian answer is not record-burning; it is the first commandment (Exo 20:3) taught with joy. Music is a gift, and the Beatles wrote some fine songs. But no performer can bear the weight of worship, and many have been crushed under it. The gospel offers what celebrity promises and cannot give: a glory that is real, a Person worthy of all devotion, and a marvel that is history, not fable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin fabula (a story) → fabulosus → English fabulous (fabled; then marvelous) → early-1960s British clip fab → 1963 "the Fab Four."

Latin fabula — a story, a fable; fabulosus — celebrated in story

English fabulous — fabled, legendary (1828); later, marvelous, incredible

Early 1960s British slang: fab

1963: the Beatles dubbed "the Fab Four"; February 9, 1964, The Ed Sullivan Show

March 1966: Lennon’s "more popular than Jesus" remark (London Evening Standard)

Usage

""Grandma still calls anything she likes ‘fab.’ She saw the Beatles at Shea Stadium in 1965 and can’t remember a single song for the screaming.""

"It is the voice of a god, and not of a man (Act 12:22) — the crowd’s error in every age."

"Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1Jn 5:21)."
